ABSTRACT
This study investigates the impact of modeling simplifications on the uncertainty of seismic response in numerical simulations,
focusing on a five-story, asymmetric-plan, reinforced-concrete building in Santiago, Chile, subjected to simulated seismic motions
from hypothetical events at the San Ramón fault (SRF). In order to achieve this, a comparative analysis is conducted between
a high-complexity reference model and lower-complexity models. The reference model incorporates three-dimensional seismic
inputs using the domain reduction method (DRM) and a detailed structural model accounting for material nonlinear behavior.
The complexity of the models is systematically reduced to assess the effects of different soil–structure interaction (SSI) modeling
assumptions. These assumptions include the use of DRM and plane-wave (PW) input, and also the exclusion of SSI through fixed-
base (FB) conditions. For each model, both linear and nonlinear material behaviors are considered. Given the lack of historical
records from the SRF, the study employs source-to-structure physical simulation to address seismic performance evaluation as
well as its sensitivity to modeling. Simulations are conducted in OpenSees using input motions from 10 realizations of a 𝑀𝑤= 6.7
event at the SRF, generated with the ShakerMaker Python library. With respect to the reference model, findings indicate that PW
assumptions moderately increase uncertainty across different engineering demand parameters (EDPs) and analysis directions.
Conversely, FB conditions significantly elevate modeling uncertainty, drastically changing the mean and variance of computed
EDPs. A simple EDP sensitivity score is proposed to compare the statistics of computed EDPs, from which a global performance-
score is constructed for ranking of models with respect to the reference model. The ranking shows that linear FB models may
outperform non-linear FB models, highlighting a complex and nonintuitive relationship between structural nonlinearity and soil
flexibility modeling on uncertainty. There are also indications that high-complexity modeling, accounting for the spatio-temporal
complexities of the seismic wave-field through the DRM, is needed for responses quantities sensitive to high frequencies. Overall,

Introduction
The field of Performance-based Earthquake Engineering (PBEE)
represents a shift towards a more refined approach in seismic
design, aiming to control the response of structures under
seismic actions more effectively. This paradigm shift seeks to
establish detailed performance objectives that go beyond mere
collapse prevention, providing stakeholders with enhanced
ability to manage the impacts of seismic events. A critical
element in realizing this vision is the accurate prediction of
how structures respond to earthquake loads, a prerequisite for
the effective implementation of PBEE principles. The ability to
predict structural behavior with precision is essential for aligning
design outcomes with the specified performance targets, thus
underscoring the significance of reliable predictive models in the
advancement of earthquake engineering [1].
When tasked with developing a numerical model for evaluating
a structure within the PBEE framework, designers encounter
a diverse array of prudential modeling choices. These choices
offer varying degrees of complexity and predictive capabilities,
necessitating a judicious balance between the resources expended
on model development, simulation and post-processing and the
fidelity of the predictions obtained. The decision-making process
may involve choosing between different modeling approaches,
such as linear versus nonlinear constitutive models, each with
its own set of assumptions about material behavior. Additionally,
the consideration of soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects [2]
introduces another layer of complexity, prompting designers to
select an appropriate modeling strategy that accounts for these
influences. This selection process is complicated by the need to
navigate various assumptions inherent in each model, which can
significantly impact the predicted structural response.
To navigate these complexities effectively, it is beneficial for
designers to have a clear understanding of how different modeling
decisions influence the accuracy and reliability of predictions.
A critical examination of modeling uncertainties, particularly
those arising from incomplete knowledge or simplified repre-
sentations of physical processes, can facilitate a more strategic
allocation of resources. This includes computational efforts, data
collection, and the development of mitigation strategies aimed
at addressing the most consequential uncertainties. Modeling
uncertainty, often referred to as epistemic uncertainty, arises
from the limitations in our understanding of the system being
modeled or the use of models that fail to fully capture the
underlying physical processes. The quest to reduce this form of
uncertainty involves the adoption of more sophisticated models
that better replicate the actual behavior of structures under
seismic loading. Recent research efforts have focused on dis-
secting and understanding the sources of modeling uncertainty,
highlighting the significant impact of SSI and non-linearity on
predictive accuracy. Ignoring soil flexibility, for example, has been
shown to introduce considerable uncertainty [3] into predictions,
a finding supported by numerous studies [4–9]. Moreover, the
choice of constitutive models for seismic response simulation
[10] and the inherent variability in seismic records [11] are
recognized as major contributors to overall modeling uncertainty.
Nonetheless, the relative influence of these factors can vary [6, 12–
14], notwithstanding that other higher-level sources of modeling
uncertainty (such as considering SSI or not, or how the seismic
input is modeled) can also lead to comparable uncertainty levels
[15]. The level of uncertainty also differs across various response
parameters [4], indicating the need for targeted approaches in
addressing the specific challenges posed by epistemic uncertainty
in structural response modeling.
The spatial variability of the incoming seismic wave field, due
to wave propagation, introduces a notable source of uncertainty
in seismic response predictions [5, 16–19]. The assumption of
earthquake waves as vertically propagating planar waves, a com-
mon simplification in many SSI studies, may lead to inaccuracies
under certain conditions. The domain reduction method (DRM),
as established by [20, 21], offers a robust approach for modeling
spatially variable seismic input, reflecting a growing interest in
its application for more accurate seismic simulations. Despite
its potential, the literature reveals a gap in uncertainty studies
that incorporate DRM for models with spatially variable inputs,
indicating an area ripe for exploration and contribution.
Selecting the appropriate modeling fidelity to meet specific
PBEE objectives is a critical decision-making process that must
be tailored to each individual system. It requires a thoughtful
analysis of the seismic loading characteristics expected and

powerful procedures to accommodate various fidelity levels in

This study presents an in-depth case analysis aimed at exploring
the trade-offs involved in different modeling approaches for
evaluating the seismic performance of a five-story reinforced
concrete (RC) structure located at the Universidad de los Andes
campus in Santiago, Chile. Central to this investigation is the
use of a high-fidelity nonlinear model employing the DRM,
designed to simulate the building’s behavior under seismic
events from a nearby shallow crustal fault—events for which
historical data do not exist. The objective is to discern how
various modeling strategies impact the statistical distribution of
EDPs against a high-fidelity reference model. To achieve this,
the study systematically examines three seismic input modeling
techniques—fixed-base (FB), plane-wave (PW), and DRM—with
DRM serving as the reference case. Figure 1 illustrates the
three modeling approaches explored herein. In addition to the
consideration of SSI and earthquake input method, this article
also delves into the influence of material behavior, comparing

Modeling
2.1
Seismic Modeling for DRM Dataset
Generation
This study focuses on a building located east of the SRF, as
depicted in Figure 2a. The building’s location is 2 km from the
fault’s northernmost surface trace and 8 km from the epicenter
designated for this study. Notably, it is positioned on the hanging
wall relative to the rupture plane. According to the Chilean
seismic design code (Nch433), the building falls within seismic
zone 1 and soil site classification B, attributing a peak-ground
acceleration (PGA) of 0.2𝑔. This PGA is primarily influenced
by subduction tectonics and is determined through uniform
hazard analyses encompassing all credible seismic sources, which
precludes shallow crustal sources like the SRF. The activity
status of the SRF remains contentious [23], with the latest event
estimated to have occurred over 9000 years ago.
Importantly, no earthquake motions have been recorded from the
SRF, making modeling and simulation the only methods available
to anticipate the potential effects of seismic activity from this
source. To date, most recent studies have relied on ground-motion
prediction equations to estimate intensity measures such as PGA.
To the authors’ knowledge, direct simulation attempts like the
one presented in this study have not been reported previously,
with all intensity estimations based on attenuation models.
Recent investigations [24–29] propose potential SRF scenarios
ranging from magnitudes 𝑀𝑤= 6.2 to 7.5. For the larger mag-
nitude events, multisegment rupturing is considered plausible.
Vargas et al. [25] estimate a PGA of 0.4𝑔at proximities of 5 km
for a magnitude 7.5 event. Estay et al. [27] predict PGAs around
0.5𝑔at the building’s location for a 𝑀𝑤= 6.7 event, considering
average shear wave velocities in the upper 30 m (𝑉𝑠30) from a
regional model developed elsewhere. Ammirati et al. [28] present
two attenuation models for a 𝑀𝑤= 7.5 scenario, forecasting PGAs
between 0.7𝑔± 0.3𝑔near the fault’s scarp and ranging from
0.6 to 0.8𝑔at the hanging wall. Yañez et al. [29] predict PGAs
between 0.33 and 0.55𝑔at 5-km distance from the fault for a
𝑀𝑤= 6.5 event.
Figure 2a provides a contextual overview of the greater Santiago
metropolitan area, including the SRF’s estimated surface trace
and the location of the studied building on the fault’s northern
hanging wall. The right panel of Figure 2 presents 10 kinematic
rupture process realizations for a 𝑀𝑤= 6.7 event on the SRF,
depicting slip distribution and rupture triggering iso-chrones at
1-s intervals. All these processes were developed using the UCSB
earthquake simulation method [30, 31], offering insights into
the variability of ground motion due to the source-component
[32] (within-event variability). Guided by known scaling laws for
crustal events, for example, Leonard et al. [33], a length of 30km
and a width of 16km, are chosen for the rupture size of this event.
This fault area is discretized into 256 faults along-strike (350◦
from north) and 128 faults along dip (40◦down-dip towards the
east, with a rake angle of 113◦). A corner frequency of 0.18 Hz
corresponding to a stress-drop of 1.28 MPa is specified also based
on the scaling relationships of Leonard et al.
Seismic motions for each scenario are simulated using the
ShakerMaker Python module [34], employing the F-K method
[35], which assumes a flat, horizontally layered, elastic crust
model. The crustal model’s top layer, aligned with local geotech-
nical studies for the building project, features a shear wave speed
𝑉𝑠= 750 m/s and a density of 𝜌= 2400 kg∕m

The kinematic source description incorporates discretized slip at
each subfault patch, their trigger-times, slip duration, and ran-
domized subfault geometries for fault roughness. The source time
function for each subfault is defined in terms of slip-rate in the
manner of Crempien et al. [31], with the peak-time (𝑡peak) to rise-
time (𝑡rise) ratio playing a crucial role in determining the earth-
quake’s high-frequency content. This ratio is fixed at 𝑡peak∕𝑡rise =
0.15, yielding PGA values in agreement with simulations for
similar events on this fault by other researchers previously
mentioned. Further details are available in Torres’ work [39].
The resultant displacement and acceleration time-histories for
the 10 source process realizations are illustrated in Figure 3.
The setup yields an average maximum horizontal PGA of
0.21𝑔± 0.05𝑔, with a maximum of 0.32𝑔across all realizations.
For these events, the significant duration is around 20 s starting at
about the 9-s mark. Finally, note that the displacement histories
show that initial motion is upward (+𝑍) and to the west (−𝑋) as
would be expected at the hanging wall of an eastward-dipping
fault with a northern strike. However the fault is not perfectly
normal (oblique average rake angle), which results in high
north–south components (±𝑌) as well as variability in the
predicted final co-seismic displacement, which will depend on
the details of the fault slip-distribution.
To enable use in the DRM, the simulated accelerations and
displacements are computed for points on a 105 × 105m “box,”
representing the volume of soil below and surrounding the
target building (see Figure 5a). These data are stored in the
H5DRM format, which is compatible with both ShakerMaker and
OpenSees [40], which is used later for the site-structure model.
The DRM applies motion within the FEA domain by converting
displacements and accelerations at the nodes into equivalent
dynamic forces. These forces act on a one-element-thick layer of
nodes, as illustrated in Figure 1c.
An important step in verifying the model setup involves ensuring
that a finite-element representation of the free field produces the
expected surface motion at a specific point within the domain.
The H5DRM format includes the predicted free-field motion at the
center of the DRM box as part of its built-in “quality-assurance”
(QA) feature. This QA motion serves as a reference for verifying
proper wave propagation conditions within the finite-element
mesh. This crucial check was performed, but is not included
herein for brevity.

Because of the DRM’s formulation, free-field conditions are only
maintained within the defined DRM box. When deviations from
the free-field condition are introduced—such as the addition of
topography or the building—motions within the DRM box will
no longer perfectly match the original free-field response. These
deviations generate motions that propagate out of the DRM box,
which must be damped in the surrounding exterior domain to
prevent spurious reflections and ensure accurate results. In the
present work, the absorbent exterior domain (AED) approach, as
explained in Pinto et al. [41], is used to damp said motions. The
exterior boundary of the DRM box is constrained by fully fixing
the displacement of the nodes on it. The absorbent boundary
is established with 20% Rayleigh damping, at 𝑓1 = 0.1 Hz and
𝑓2 = 10 Hz, and a length of 10 elements to mitigate spurious
reflections of outgoing waves (radiation damping) at the domain
edges. Inside the DRM box, 2% Rayleigh damping at the same
frequencies is assigned to the solid elements to account for
small-strain energy dissipation in the soil.
2.2
Structural and Near-Field Site Modeling
The finite element model developed herein is an extension of the
one elaborated in the final graduation project of Hurtado [42].
This section explains the key aspects of the model, while the
reader is referred to the cited work (available upon request) for
more detail.
Referenced in Figure 4a is a photo of the “Engineering Building”
housing the Faculty of Engineering and Applied Sciences at
Universidad de los Andes, Chile, which constitutes the focal
point of this investigation. Adjacent to this (b), the geometric
model of the building, developed in STKO, is shown. This
geometric model serves as a precursor to the development of
an OpenSees model used for analysis. Figure 4c expands on
this depiction, illustrating a broader perspective of the geometric
model that incorporates both a soil box and adjacent topography
and providing information regarding the meshing, element, and
constitutive model choices in each part. The highlighted red
region indicates the area where soil motions are generated using
the DRM. The soil domain outside the DRM box (AED) is meshed
with standard eight-node bricks (stdBrick in OpenSees). Within
the DRM box, the intricate geometry of the topography and the
proximal regions of the building are meshed using standard four-
node tetrahedron (FourNodeTetrahedron) elements. A general
view of the FE mesh is shown in Figure 5b. The soil behavior
is modeled throughout using an elastic isotropic material model,
with properties based on the ShakerMaker output for the upper
soil layers, assumed to be uniform across the site. Consequently,
this study does not consider the effects of spatial variability
or heterogeneity within the soil. Accounting for these varia-
tions would require generating separate ground motion datasets
for each combination of soil properties, which would become
computationally prohibitive.
Wall and slab elements are modeled using ASDShellQ4 shell
elements. The shear walls are composed of a layered cross-
section, with different materials used to represent concrete or
steel rebars. The concrete’s constitutive response is modeled using
the ASDConcrete3D model, employing IMPL-EX integration [43]
for fast convergence and global algorithmic robustness, while the
steel reinforcement is represented using the Hysteretic uniaxial
material model. This steel model allows precise control of the
post-yield behavior of the rebars, especially the pinching effect
for post-buckling response. The layered shell cross section used
to represent the walls was set up with eight layers, with the steel
layer thickness calculated to represent the total longitudinal
reinforcement present in the walls. On the other hand, the
ASDConcrete3D model, when used from within STKO, provides
a convenient feature that prevents mesh-dependent strain-
localization due to its strain-softening behavior. This is done by
adjusting the fracture energy of the constitutive model using a
characteristic element length at each finite element. Floor slabs
are modeled using elastic properties without the assumption of
a rigid diaphragm. The beams and beam columns are modeled
using dispBeamColumn elements with fiber cross-sections,
employing TC1D concrete and Steel02 (Giuffré–Menegotto–
Pinto) material models to simulate the stress–strain response of

All shallow foundations are modeled with elastic standard-brick
elements (3-DOF per node). As shown in Figure 6, these elements
are connected to the building shells (walls) and beams (6-DOF
per node) using beam-to-solid coupling. This STKO feature (inter-
action) automatically creates new nodes and applies equalDOF or
rigidLink constraints to ensure a correct transfer of rotational
DOFs from a solid face to an edge or node of a quadrilateral. All
such interactions are depicted in Figure 5c, where the purple lines
indicate the kinematic constraints. In addition, the foundations
are connected to the soil through an ASDEmbeddedNodeElement
condition, which ensures a connection between the retained
and constrained nodes regardless of the mesh size or element
type. That constraint ensures displacement compatibility at the
embedded node through a penalty formulation. Finally, another
embedded node condition is used to connect the mesh coming
from the free field, with the finer mesh required near the
building foundations.
Mass distribution within the model is assigned based on material
densities for solid elements and equivalent area and line
densities derived from the cross-sectional properties of shell and
line elements. In accordance with Chilean design standards,
50% of live loads are assumed to be present on the building slabs
during transient analysis. Additionally, a 5% Rayleigh damping
is applied to the structure using the same frequencies as before.
The mesh size for the building and near-field soil is set
at 1 m. For the far-field, a mesh size of 2.5 m is adopted,
in line with the Courant–Lewy–Friedrichs [44] (CFL) condi-
tions for resolving wave propagation up to 20 Hz. Dynamic
simulations are executed with a time step of 𝑑𝑡= 0.0025 s,
utilizing a variable time-step transient integration scheme
and the Hilber–Hughes–Taylor algorithm to ensure solution
robustness. The mesh for the DRM model consists of 153,700

This high-fidelity DRM model is subsequently simplified into
a PW model, where input occurs at the base in the form of
traction forces proportional to particle velocity at depth, assuming
planar and vertically propagating input waves. In this config-
uration, horizontal motions are attributed to shear waves, and
vertical motions to compression waves. To eliminate spurious
reflections at domain boundaries, absorbing boundary elements
(ASDAbsorbingBoundary [45]) are employed instead of the AED
used with the DRM. Additionally, because a PW is assumed, the
mesh is allowed to have a coarser discretization in the horizontal
directions, which reduces the number of nodes and elements.
The mesh for the PW model consists of 82,585 nodes, resulting
in 305,247 degrees-of-freedom connecting 179,563 elements.

The model is further simplified into a FB model, wherein the soil
and foundations are excluded, and the base nodes of walls and
columns are fixed. The input in this scenario is the acceleration
time-history recorded at the surface of the free-field problem. It is
critical to note that in all models, the input motion is configured to
replicate the unperturbed free-field motion, ensuring consistent
consideration of site response effects. Thus, any differences in
response are attributable to the specifics of the input models
rather than site effects, facilitating a comprehensive comparison.
The mesh for the FB model consists of 18,995 nodes, resulting in
113,970 degrees-of-freedom connecting 21,164 elements.
Finally, elastic variants of the DRM, PW, and FB models are
created by assigning elastic materials to the corresponding con-
stitutive properties. This implies that uncracked properties were
used for these analysis.
A modal analysis was conducted on the elastic FB model,
revealing the first three mode shapes and their corresponding
periods, as illustrated in Figure 7. The structural asymmetry of
the building induces torsional coupling across all modes. The
primary mode is characterized by translational motion along
the 𝑌-axis, complemented by a torsional component, yielding a
period of 𝑇1 = 0.570 s. The subsequent mode exhibits a predomi-
nantly torsional behavior, with notable translational movements
in both the 𝑋- and 𝑌-directions, resulting in a period of 𝑇2 =
0.498 s. The third mode predominantly features translational
motion along the 𝑋-axis, albeit with a discernible degree of
torsional coupling, underscoring the complex dynamic behavior
of the structure. Due to the size of the models that incorporate the
soil domain, a modal analysis for these models was not feasible.
Herein, the models utilizing the DRM to excite response are
considered the high-fidelity reference model to which all other
models are compared. The PW model is thought of as a state-of-
the-art model which incorporates SSI and is essentially equivalent
in all respects to the DRM model, except in input and handling
of boundary conditions. The FB model is a state-of-practice
model which, in its linear variant, is similar to the one used
to design the building according to standard Chilean practice.

2.3
Computational Cost
Each model type (DRM, PW, and FB, nonlinear and elastic)
was simulated for 10 realizations of the input motion, resulting
in a total of 60 simulations. These computational experiments
were conducted on OpenSeesMP within the high-performance
computing (HPC) Linux cluster “Esmeralda” at Universidad de
los Andes. The cluster consists of gaming workstations equipped
with AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processors and 64GB of
RAM, interconnected through a 2.5-GbE network, with 10-GbE
transfer rates for I/O. The domain was decomposed into 16
partitions, determined to be optimal for the hardware and the
models’ computational requirements, particularly given the high
computational cost of assembling and solving the global stiffness
system-of-equations. It might be useful to note that, in the
experience of the authors, most of the compute time is spent on
the assembly and solution of the global system of equations when,
and this drives computational cost. The cost of I/O for these
models is around 10% of compute time.
To facilitate comparison, the Table 2 summarizes the computa-
tional costs for each model type, including execution times for
nonlinear and elastic variants, and relative differences in compu-
tational time with respect to the elastic FB model as reference.
The total compute CPU-time for the final runs in this study was
approximately 64.53 days, while the wall time amounted to about
2weeks thanks to the use of HPC. Logically, the actual compute
time is higher due to test runs used in setting up the model. This
underscores the importance of HPC in advancing performance-
based engineering, particularly in handling computationally
expensive nonlinear models. The seismic response outcomes of
these models, both in linear and nonlinear variants, are analyzed
and discussed in the subsequent section.
3
Results and Discussion
In this section, the response of the different models subjected
to earthquake loading simulated from 10 realizations of an
earthquake with a moment magnitude 𝑀𝑤= 6.7 on the SRF is
examined. The analysis focuses on EDPs, presenting ensemble
averages and standard deviations for each EDP as a function
of time, periods, or as scalar maximum absolute values. The
nonlinear model using the DRM is taken as the reference case
for comparing EDPs. Even though this model has the potential
to be the highest fidelity model, extensive validation of all
components is needed for this to be the case. Hence, what follows
is an exercise in determining and understanding how different
modeling assumptions impact the computed EDPs and their
statistics, which are used to derive fragility curves in PBEE. The
analysis leaves out important sources of uncertainty such as
soil heterogeneity and nonlinearity, material (parametric) uncer-
tainty and epistemic (modeling) uncertainty in the constitutive
models, and mass uncertainty to name a few.
Initially, EDPs are introduced, then the results are shown and
discussed. A more detailed statistical analysis is then conducted
for selected EDPs, culminating in a discussion of the main
global observations.

Figure 10 shows the time evolution of tension damage for one
realization of the FB and DRM models. The compression (𝑑−)
and tension (𝑑+) damage variables are a measure of the stiffness
loss in each case according to the original implementation of
ASDConcrete3D [43]. Tension damage occurs most severely at the
lower levels, where the walls connect to the (elastic) slabs. Apart
from the intensity differences between the FB and DRM models,
there are no obvious differences in damage distributions. The
state of tension damage of the FB model at 17.5 s is similar to that
of the DRM model at 22.5 s, with the DRM model showing less
damage overall. It is important to emphasize that tension damage
implies tension cracking, with steel rebars taking the load instead,
and does not imply loss in capacity. The overall translational
stiffness of the structure would not be largely affected by tension
damage. However, it would be expected that tension damage
influences the torsional stiffness of the building. Compression
damage, which would lead to real loss of capacity and impact the
building translational stiffness, was minimal and restricted to the
bottom of the flag-shaped shear-wall along the 𝑋-axis.

Torsional Response Analysis
Figure 14 presents the time history of the absolute torsion angle’s
mean value plus or minus one standard deviation, as measured
by the rotational degree of freedom around the 𝑍-axis at the
building’s top floor center of mass. Torsional response promotes
an irregular distribution of drifts across the building’s plan,
which can lead to irregular damage patterns, particularly in
nonstructural elements, in structures with significant torsional
eccentricities like the one under study. Interestingly, the FB
model forecasts greater torsional rotation than both the PW

models exhibit greater dispersion in their responses compared
to their linear counterparts, whereas the FB model shows more
dispersion in the nonlinear response at early times and the
elastic response demonstrates more variance at later stages.

responses, underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling
the soil domain to accurately capture the torsional behavior. In
all, FB modeling seems to exacerbate the torsional response of
the structure.

Significance and Effect Size Analysis
Because they produce visually similar results, it is hard to com-
pare the nonlinear DRM and PW model predictions, for exam-
ple, for pseudo spectral response (Figure 9b,e), drift response
(Figures 12b,d and 13b,d), and torsion response (Figure 14).
A finer analysis is needed to better understand the statistical
performance of these seemingly similar models. The tools to
do this are significance testing with Student’s T-test [47] and
effect size testing with Cohen’s D parameter [48], related but
complimentary statistical indicators. Student’s T-test compares
the means of two samples and determines the probability that the
observed differences are due to chance; lower Student’s T-test 𝑝
values indicate that there is a low chance that differences are due
to randomness. Cohen’s D provides a measure of the effect size,
or the magnitude of difference between two groups, in a way that
is independent of the sample size. It also shows the direction of
the effect (or bias) allowing for a more intuitive understanding of
the practical significance of the findings.
Figure 15 the per-period 𝑝values of a T-test applied to the pseudo-

that the differences in mean are significant for all EDPs, but the
same is not true for the PW model.
Student’s T-test 𝑝values are nontrivially related to effect size
and also the sample size. Cohen’s D parameter is only related
to effect size and direction of change. Figure 16 shows similar
plots using Cohen’s D parameter, it is amplitude indicates the

For low periods (subfigures (a) and (d)), the effect size is rather
large, despite inconclusive T-test results, it can be said that the
PW values are noticeably higher than DRM results (FB results are

show diminishing effects sizes once damage is done evolving,
probably related to the elongation of periods after damage which

3.7
Discussion
The analysis of building EDPs, such as those discussed herein, is
central to performance-based and fragility assessments in earth-
quake engineering. These assessments are not only prevalent in
academic literature but are also a part of ongoing professional
practice. The case study building, though not overly complex and
situated on competent soil where site nonlinearity is anticipated
to be minimal in influencing system response, underscores the
significance of incorporating foundation, soil, and site response
modeling for accurate prediction of EDPs of interest.
The findings demonstrate the limitations of FB modeling, which
exhibits significant, systematic biases and unintuitive variabil-
ity changes in system response. This variability and bias are
dependent on the direction of analysis and the specific EDP;
for spectral EDPs, the variation even extends across different
periods. This is exemplified in the divergent behaviors observed in
floor PSA spectral responses and drift responses across directions:

softer soil sites where the shorter seismic wavelengths for the

the relationship between the DRM and PW models.

prevent spurious reflections. Tools like STKO and corresponding

verified simulation results, and shared in formats like H5DRM to
broaden their applicability and impact.

reflect an equally large modeling fidelity gap between these mod-

in a simplified manner could offer a viable compromise between
predictive accuracy and modeling or computational efficiency.

In terms of nonlinearity, the moderate earthquake magnitude
and corresponding local intensity mobilized only limited struc-
tural nonlinearity. Nevertheless, the results show that elastic
models produce very different results for certain EDPs, such as
the shape of floor pseudo-spectral ordinates, when compared
to the reference model. While mean drift responses appear
similar—supported by Student’s T-tests that do not reject the
null hypothesis—Cohen’s D-parameters indicate discrepancies
in predicting response variability with elastic models, suggesting
the need for nonlinear modeling to capture the full spectrum of
structural responses accurately, at least for the EDPs under con-
sideration.
While the Student’s T-test and Cohen’s D provide foundational
statistical analyses—identifying whether model differences are
significant and the size of these differences, respectively—the
similarity analysis adds a layer by evaluating the degree of
convergence between model predictions within the context of
their CIs. This approach allows for a more practical assessment
of model reliability and applicability by directly quantifying
how well the models agree across their entire range of predic-
tions, rather than focusing solely on mean differences or their
statistical significance.
A limitation of the present study is the narrow scope of single-
event variability, as only 10 realizations were generated for a
single seismic scenario on the SRF. Record-to-record variability—
a major contributor to aleatory uncertainty in PBEE—was not
the primary focus of this work. Instead, this study concentrated
on epistemic uncertainty associated with modeling assumptions,
including ground motion generation, structural nonlinearity, and
SSI, while accounting for variability in the rupture process at a
single magnitude and rupture mode.
Additionally, this study did not address epistemic and aleatory
uncertainties related to soil variability and nonlinear soil
response. The propagation properties of upper soil strata can
exhibit a range of elastic properties, which may also vary spatially.
The authors posit that a shift toward softer soil properties would
likely result in greater divergence between the results of the
DRM model and those of the PW approximation, and an even
larger disparity with the FB model. Other unconsidered sources
of uncertainty include parametric uncertainty in all constitutive
models (e.g., concrete, steel, and soil), modeling uncertainties in
building details (e.g., connections and the number of shell layers),
and the nonlinearity of the slabs, among others.

Conclusions
This study systematically explored the impact of modeling sim-
plifications on the seismic response predictions of a reinforced
concrete building, focusing on variations of the computed EDPs
and their statistical characteristics across FB, PW, and DRM
modeling approaches. Linear and nonlinear versions of the
models were also included as possible simplifications. Through
multiple realizations of seismic motions from a hypothetical
magnitude 6.7 earthquake, it quantified the influence of these
modeling choices on the accuracy and uncertainty of structural
response metrics by using the nonlinear DRM-based model as a
reference to track changes in EDP statistics.
Key findings indicate that simplifications significantly affect the
predicted seismic responses, with the FB model introducing
the most considerable uncertainty and bias, particularly in the
direction of analysis and specific EDPs. The PW model, while
more accurate than FB approaches, still shows discrepancies
when compared to the reference DRM model, especially at
higher frequencies where DRM’s detailed wave-field represen-
tation becomes critical. However, the DRM model affirmed
the adequacy of PW modeling for many practical applications,
highlighting a reduced sensitivity to the complexities of seismic
wave propagation in certain scenarios.
The research underscores the importance of carefully selecting
modeling strategies in earthquake engineering to balance com-
putational efficiency with the need for accurate and reliable
seismic performance assessments. Future studies could further
refine these models and explore intermediate-fidelity approaches
that incorporate simplified soil flexibility, potentially offering a
viable compromise between detailed, high-fidelity models and
the computational simplicity of lower-fidelity approximations.

Abstract: This study investigates the impact of modeling simplifications on the uncertainty of seismic response in numerical simulations, focusing on a five-story, asymmetric-plan, reinforced-concrete building in Santiago, Chile, subjected to simulated seismic motions from hypothetical events at the San Ramón fault (SRF). In order to achieve this, a comparative analysis is conducted between a high-complexity reference model and lower-complexity models. The reference model incorporates three-dimensional seismic inputs using the domain reduction method (DRM) and a detailed structural model accounting for material nonlinear behavior. The complexity of the models is systematically reduced to assess the effects of different soil–structure interaction (SSI) modeling assumptions. These assumptions include the use of DRM and plane-wave (PW) input, and also the exclusion of SSI through fixed- base (FB) conditions. For each model, both linear and nonlinear material behaviors are considered. Given the lack of historical records from the SRF, the study employs source-to-structure physical simulation to address seismic performance evaluation as well as its sensitivity to modeling. Simulations are conducted in OpenSees using input motions from 10 realizations of a 𝑀𝑤= 6.7 event at the SRF, generated with the ShakerMaker Python library. With respect to the reference model, findings indicate that PW assumptions moderately increase uncertainty across different engineering demand parameters (EDPs) and analysis directions. Conversely, FB conditions significantly elevate modeling uncertainty, drastically changing the mean and variance of computed EDPs. A simple EDP sensitivity score is proposed to compare the statistics of computed EDPs, from which a global performance- score is constructed for ranking of models with respect to the reference model. The ranking shows that linear FB models may outperform non-linear FB models, highlighting a complex and nonintuitive relationship between structural nonlinearity and soil flexibility modeling on uncertainty. There are also indications that high-complexity modeling, accounting for the spatio-temporal complexities of the seismic wave-field through the DRM, is needed for responses quantities sensitive to high frequencies.
